newsitem.title: FRANCE: French port to load wheat for Iraq under U.N. plan.
newsitem.headline: French port to load wheat for Iraq under U.N. plan.

text.p: The French port of Nantes was due to start loading wheat for Iraq on Monday under a major programme of French wheat sales to help relieve the plight of Iraqis hit by international sanctions, freight sources said.

The freighter Adonis was due to load 25,000 tonnes of wheat in western France in one of the first commercial grain shipments to Iraq under an oil-for-food agreement between Iraq and the United Nations, they said.
"The Adonis is in port at the moment. It will begin loading on Monday at Nantes and finish loading at (the nearby port of) Montoire," a local freight official said late on Friday.
U.N. Secretary General Kofi Annan said in Paris on Saturday that the first deliveries of relief aid to Iraq under the oil-for-food deal would be delayed for 10 days.
"Unfortunately, there has been a little delay, but everything is going to begin in 10 days," Annan told reporters after talks with French President Jacques Chirac.
"I have just learned of this. I do not know the reasons for the delay," Annan said.

Under the oil-for-food deal, Iraq is permitted to sell $2 billion worth of oil over six months to buy needed supplies for its people, who have suffered under sanctions since Iraq's invasion of Kuwait in August 1990.
The complex deal involves U.N. monitors checking on food, medicine and other goods for the Iraqi people.
Annan, who was in Paris for talks with French officials on a broad range of U.N.-related matters, had said on Thursday that the food deliveries to Iraq would begin on Saturday.
Grain exporters sold 600,000 tonnes of French wheat to Iraq in December and January but so far only 100,000 tonnes have been given the necessary approval by U.N. inspectors in New York.
Iraq has complained that the distribution of supplies has been too slow in starting.
Unconfirmed reports say 35,000 tonnes of French wheat had already left Nantes for Iraq in mid-February.

A spokesman for Annan on Saturday denied an Iraqi report that Baghdad was in negotiations to increase its income from the oil-for-food deal with the United Nations, a move that would allow it to increase its purchases of food and medicine.
"The secretary-general says there are no discussions that he has had with the Iraqis about raising the ceiling over six months," Annan's spokesman Fred Eckhard told Reuters in Paris.

Eckhard was responding to a statement by Iraqi Oil Minister Amir Muhammad Rasheed, who said in Baghdad on Friday that Iraq was negotiating with the United Nations to increase its income under U.N. resolution 986.
France, which has conditionally backed an easing of wider economic sanctions against Iraq, is among the countries seen most likely to benefit from grain and oil deals with Baghdad.
It has previously shipped some wheat to Iraq during the six-year blockade but these have been sent as aid or else as commercial deals under existing U.N. rules, grain traders said.
The grain sales that followed the oil-for-food pact are however thought to be the largest international food deals with Iraq since the 1991 Gulf war.
